newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian central bank policy raises questions.
newsitem.headline: Canadian central bank policy raises questions.

text.p: Any move by the Bank of Canada to begin raising interest rates would be welcomed by capital markets, but may arouse controversy in a country grappling with high unemployment and new signs of economic fragility.

"One thing that we know for sure is that if you raise rates, you choke off employment growth," Duncan Cameron, president of the Canadian Center for Policy Alternatives, said in a telephone interview on Thursday.
The Canadian unemployment rate stands at 9.6 percent and has hovered between nine and 10 percent for more than two years -- almost twice the 4.9 percent jobless rate in the United States.
But last week, the Bank of Canada made a major policy change when it said it had ended a long stretch of lowering interest rates to stimulate the sluggish domestic economy.
Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen indicated that the lower rates had worked their magic and said the Canadian economy was poised to grow by about four percent in 1997.
The bank cited recent rapid growth in the money supply as an indication the economy was growing well but cautioned that inflation could revive if the money supply was allowed to continue expanding.
"They figure there's some kind of inflationary pressure under every rock," said Cameron.
Economists widely expect the bank to allow monetary conditions to tighten, either by allowing the currency to appreciate or by slowly raising rates later this year.

"Of course it's always very controversial," Nesbitt Burns chief economist Sherry Cooper said in a recent interview. But, she added, the Canadian economy had enough momentum to digest tighter monetary conditions.
The Canadian dollar and bond markets have rallied on Thiessen's comments, bolstered by the fact that the U.S. Federal Reserve decided not to raise rates this week.

However, higher rates or tighter monetary conditions might come too soon for unemployed Canadians and uncertain consumers. While some economic indicators point to healthy economic growth in Canada, other statistics released this week suggest a more fragile economy.

Retail sales have been volatile, falling 0.8 percent in March after two months of rising. Wholesale trade dropped 2.7 percent in March. Although the trade surplus rose slightly in March to C$3.12 billion ($2.28 billion), the increase was due mainly to a drop in imports, rather than a big rise in exports.
If Thiessen allows tighter monetary conditions, "he's going to scare consumers," Cameron said. "I'd say the economic situation is largely characterized by deflationary pressures."
Thiessen has repeatedly assured Canadians that the job market was improving. He has said low interest rates had a 12 to 18 month lag in helping to boost job creation.

"He understands that unemployment is still a problem," said Ruth Getter, chief economist at Toronto-Dominion Bank. "But there are a lot of areas where the economy is showing real strength. He's treading a very fine line."
Most economists predict Canada will see about 250,000 jobs created in 1997 -- just enough to absorb new people joining the workforce.

Part of the reason the Canadian economy seemed to be growing while the job market was stagnant was that companies were investing in equipment and labor-saving machinery rather than hiring, economists said.
